properties.content: Question: cancer in the uterus Answer: Uterine cancer, also known as endometrial cancer, is a disease where cancer cells form in the tissues of the uterus (womb). It's the most common cancer of the female reproductive system. There are two main types: endometrial cancer (most common) and uterine sarcoma (rare). Endometrial cancer develops in the lining of the uterus (endometrium). Uterine sarcoma is a rare cancer that develops in the muscle wall of the uterus. Symptoms:: - Unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge, including bleeding after menopause or between periods. - Pelvic pain or pressure. - Pain during intercourse. Risk Factors:: Older age (most common in women over 50), Obesity, Hormone replacement therapy (estrogen-only), Certain inherited conditions like Lynch syndrome, and Endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the uterine lining). Diagnosis:: - Physical examination and ultrasound. - A tissue sample (biopsy) is needed for a definitive diagnosis. - Pap smears are not used to diagnose uterine cancer. Treatment:: - Surgery (hysterectomy) to remove the uterus, cervix, and possibly ovaries and fallopian tubes. - Radiation therapy. - Chemotherapy. - Hormone therapy. Outcomes:: - Five-year survival rates vary greatly depending on the stage at diagnosis. - Localized (stage 1 and 2) cancers have a 95% five-year survival rate. - Stage 4 cancers have a 18% five-year survival rate.

Question: cancer in the uterus

Answer: Uterine cancer, also known as endometrial cancer, is a disease where cancer cells form in the tissues of the uterus (womb). It's the most common cancer of the female reproductive system. There are two main types: endometrial cancer (most common) and uterine sarcoma (rare). Endometrial cancer develops in the lining of the uterus (endometrium). Uterine sarcoma is a rare cancer that develops in the muscle wall of the uterus.
Symptoms::
- Unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge, including bleeding after menopause or between periods.
- Pelvic pain or pressure.
- Pain during intercourse.
Risk Factors::
Older age (most common in women over 50), Obesity, Hormone replacement therapy (estrogen-only), Certain inherited conditions like Lynch syndrome, and Endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the uterine lining).
Diagnosis::
- Physical examination and ultrasound.
- A tissue sample (biopsy) is needed for a definitive diagnosis.
- Pap smears are not used to diagnose uterine cancer.
Treatment::
- Surgery (hysterectomy) to remove the uterus, cervix, and possibly ovaries and fallopian tubes.
- Radiation therapy.
- Chemotherapy.
- Hormone therapy.
Outcomes::
- Five-year survival rates vary greatly depending on the stage at diagnosis.
- Localized (stage 1 and 2) cancers have a 95% five-year survival rate.
- Stage 4 cancers have a 18% five-year survival rate.
